examples.question_text: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\underset{\sim}{a}=-8\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j}$. Give your answer in exact form.

Given $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-7\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$, find the exact unit vector in the direction of $\underset{\sim}{w}=\underset{\sim}{u}+\underset{\sim}{v}$.
The unit vector in the direction of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is $\frac{1}{5}(-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ and $|\underset{\sim}{a}|=15$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
examples.solution_text:
Multiply the unit vector by the required magnitude.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}&=|\underset{\sim}{a}|\,\hat{\underset{\sim}{a}}\\&=15\times\frac15(-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\\&=-9\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: The vector $\underset{\sim}{a}=k\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j}$ has magnitude $13$, where $k<0$. Find the unit vector in its direction.
examples.solution_text:
Use the magnitude to find the missing component.
$\begin{aligned}k^2+12^2&=13^2\\k^2&=25\end{aligned}$
Since $k<0$, $k=-5$.
$\begin{aligned}\hat{\underset{\sim}{a}}&=\frac{\underset{\sim}{a}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}|}\\&=\frac{1}{13}(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Determine whether $\underset{\sim}{p}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\mathbf{i}+\frac12\mathbf{j}$ is a unit vector.
examples.solution_text:
Calculate its magnitude.
$\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{p}|&=\sqrt{\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2}\\&=\sqrt{\frac34+\frac14}\\&=1\end{aligned}$
Its magnitude is $1$, so it is a unit vector.

examples.derivation: Magnitude sqrt(64+36)=10. Dividing (-8,-6) by 10 gives (-4/5,-3/5), whose squared components sum to 1. The diagram vectors (-8,-6) and (-0.8,-0.6) have the same direction and length ratio 10:1, consistent with source lines 2418–2428 and attached Image #35.

Adding components gives w=(2-7,1+3)=(-5,4). Its magnitude is sqrt(25+16)=sqrt(41), so its unit vector is (-5i+4j)/sqrt(41). Squared components sum to 41/41=1. This follows source question 2(c), lines 2455–2463.

The supplied direction vector (-3/5,4/5) has magnitude 1. Multiplying by 15 gives a=(-9,12), with magnitude sqrt(81+144)=15 and the supplied direction. This follows source question 3, lines 2466–2470.

The magnitude condition gives k²+144=169, hence k²=25. Since k<0, k=-5. Normalising gives (-5i+12j)/13, whose squared components sum to 169/169=1. The changed sign condition preserves the method of source question 4, lines 2472–2480.

The squared components are 3/4 and 1/4, so the magnitude is sqrt(1)=1. Therefore p is a unit vector. This combines the magnitude method at lines 2099–2121 with the unit-vector definition at lines 2373–2379.
